title: Coastal town after fluoridation ended: a decision citing a non-existent claim refused, qualitative design accepted, cited abstract replaced after acceptance
notes: Adversarial path on a clear qualitative question (routing qualitative, explicit under both classifier rules): a dental public health consultant studies how families and professionals see the end of water fluoridation. A fixture search returns seven records; the appraisal records five claims whose passages and numbers occur in the cited abstracts. The first design reply rests only on 'c6', which is not in the ledger, and on a figure (decay doubled) that no record or local fact reports: the id is dropped with an issue, the decision is left with no claim, and the investigator's acceptance must be refused (G7; S1, S8). The investigator withdraws it, and the revised reply rests on c3 to c5 with the ethics gate unknown and the budget gate met on the investigator's own constraint; acceptance is a supported positive with the action blocked. While still on Design, the journal's corrected abstract for the parent survey cited by c3 reverses its key figure: the decision must become stale and blocked, completed stages after Scan are flagged, and this survives reload and appears in the export. The change uses field 'abstract', which D1 adds; the scenario does not assert the abstract's stored representation. Record ids were computed by a generator script that loads stableRecordId from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59: normalised-DOI hash for records 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 (ev-18pbfql, ev-0cq2ez1, ev-024im1i, ev-0qopbqo, ev-0dfumpb, ev-1vd798v) and titleYearKey hash for record 5 (ev-1bpruyv). Requires S1 and S8 (refusal), S10 (revision covers source text), S11, S13, D1 and D5. inputs.need:
I am a consultant in dental public health for a region that includes a coastal town of about 48,000 people. In March 2023 the town council voted to stop community water fluoridation after a long public campaign, and dosing ended in September 2023. Our school dental checks show that the proportion of five-year-olds with visible tooth decay rose from 21 percent in 2022 to 27 percent in 2025, but the numbers are small and the checks changed provider in 2024, so I do not want to build a causal claim on them.

What the council, the dental practices and I do not understand is how families and local professionals see the decision now: whether parents know that fluoridation has stopped, what they do instead (fluoride toothpaste, varnish at the dentist, nothing), why some groups campaigned so hard against it, and how trust in the council and in dental advice has changed. The council is considering a new public consultation in 2027, and I want our communication to rest on what people actually think, not on what we assume.

We would like to conduct a qualitative study with interviews and focus groups with parents of young children, dentists and dental nurses, school nurses, councillors and campaigners on both sides. I need help with sampling so that we hear from the families with the highest decay rates and not only the most vocal, how to handle a polarised topic safely, how many interviews are realistic, and how to relate what we hear to the dental data without overclaiming. We have a small budget for interpreters and transcription and about eight months.
inputs.constraints: Budget of 6,000 for interpreters, transcription and participant vouchers; eight months from January 2027; no new clinical examination of children; the team takes no role in the council's consultation campaign.
localFacts: The town council voted on 2023-03-14 to end community water fluoridation; dosing stopped in September 2023.
School dental checks recorded visible decay in 21 percent of five-year-olds in 2022 and 27 percent in 2025; the check provider changed in 2024.
The application to the regional research ethics committee was submitted on 2026-09-01 (REC-2026-0412); no decision has been received.
The council's communications office agreed to share anonymised consultation responses from 2022 and 2023 (letter COMMS-2026-08).

records.title: Dental caries in children after cessation of community water fluoridation: a comparison of two cities
records.authors: Brannigan-Oyelowo S, Lindqvist-Amadi P, Ferro-Mackenzie T
records.abstract: We compared dental caries in children aged 7 to 10 in a city that stopped community water fluoridation with a city that continued it, using school dental examinations before and five years after cessation. Decay-affected surfaces rose by 0.7 per child in the city that stopped, with no change in the comparison city. The increase was largest in children eligible for free school meals. The two cities differed in dental service provision, and examiners were not blinded to city. Dental attendance fell slightly in both cities over the period.

records.title: Public attitudes to community water fluoridation: a qualitative study of a contested local decision
records.abstract: We interviewed 36 residents, councillors and health professionals in a town that debated ending fluoridation. Views on fluoridation were shaped more by trust in the council and in experts than by evidence about teeth. Opponents framed fluoridation as a question of choice and consent; supporters framed it as fairness for children who do not see a dentist. Both sides described the consultation as adversarial. Parents with young children were under-represented, and no interviews were held in languages other than English.

records.title: Parents' knowledge of fluoridation status and use of fluoride toothpaste: a cross-sectional survey
records.abstract: We surveyed 1,212 parents of children under five in three areas with different fluoridation histories. Only 38 percent of parents knew whether their water was fluoridated, and knowledge was lowest in the most deprived areas. Parents who knew their water was not fluoridated were no more likely to use fluoride toothpaste of adequate strength. Most parents took advice on toothpaste from pharmacies and supermarkets rather than from dental teams. Response was lower in deprived areas. The authors recommend telling families directly when the fluoridation status of their water changes.

records.title: Dentists' responses to the end of water fluoridation: interviews in general dental practice
records.abstract: We interviewed 22 dentists and dental nurses in practices serving a town where fluoridation had recently ended. Participants described increasing fluoride varnish for young children but lacked appointments to reach families who did not attend. Several felt that public health teams had left them to explain the decision to parents without support. Participants disagreed about whether to raise fluoridation with parents at all. Most practices had long waiting lists for new child patients. Some participants had stopped mentioning fluoridation to avoid arguments with parents.

records.title: Inequalities in child dental extractions after fluoridation cessation: an interrupted time series
records.abstract: We used hospital records of dental extractions under general anaesthesia in children for eight years around the end of fluoridation in one region. Extraction rates rose after cessation, with the largest increase in the most deprived quintile (rate ratio 1.46) and little change in the least deprived quintile (rate ratio 1.05). A concurrent change in the referral pathway may explain part of the rise. Extractions are a late and severe outcome and miss most decay. The authors call for earlier measures of decay, such as school examinations, to monitor the effects of cessation.

records.title: Misinformation and trust in local fluoridation debates: content analysis of public consultation responses
records.authors: Hallorann-Ito K, Mensah-Duarte R, Lindgren-Okafor B
records.abstract: We analysed 1,960 written responses to a council consultation on community water fluoridation. In all, 42 percent of responses cited health fears not supported by the evidence reviewed by the council, and 27 percent questioned the council's honesty rather than the science. Responses in favour of fluoridation were shorter and more often cited children's teeth. Few responses came from parents of young children or from people in the most deprived neighbourhoods. The authors recommend engagement that starts from trust, not from correcting facts.

records.title: Community engagement methods for contested public health decisions: a scoping review
records.abstract: We mapped methods used to engage communities in contested public health decisions such as fluoridation, vaccination programmes and speed limits. We included 31 studies. Deliberative methods, such as citizens' panels, reached a broader range of residents than open consultations, which were dominated by organised groups. Few studies evaluated whether engagement changed decisions or trust. Studies rarely reported how they reached people with low literacy or limited English. The authors suggest planning engagement before a decision is framed, with explicit steps to reach residents who do not usually respond to consultations.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Comparative studies suggest that decay and extractions rise after fluoridation stops, most in deprived children, though confounded by service changes. Qualitative and consultation studies show that views are driven by trust and framed as choice against fairness, that many parents do not know their fluoridation status, and that open consultations are dominated by organised groups while parents of young children and deprived families are rarely heard. Dental teams feel left to explain the decision. No retrieved study reports the views of families after cessation in their own words.
response.gradeRationale: Observational comparisons with confounding for outcomes; single-site qualitative and content analyses for views; consistent themes but limited transferability.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five source-derived claims; overall certainty low.

steps.note: Appraisal of the seven retrieved records (S13); five claims whose passages and numbers occur in the cited abstracts. Certainty low over inspected records (G1).

contexts: school dental checks with a provider change
response.reading: Two different questions are tangled: whether decay rises after cessation, which comparative evidence suggests and local data cannot settle, and how people understand and act on the decision, which no retrieved study answers for families after cessation. Trust links the council, dental teams and families; open consultations amplify organised groups and leave out the parents whose children are most at risk.

response.overview: Qualitative study with one-to-one interviews and role-specific focus groups in a coastal town after fluoridation ended, analysed with reflexive thematic analysis.
response.population: Parents of children under eight (purposively sampled across deprivation quintiles, with at least half from the two most deprived), dentists and dental nurses, school nurses, councillors, and campaigners for and against fluoridation.
response.exposure: Living or working in the town after fluoridation ended in September 2023.
response.procedures: Recruitment through children's centres, school nurses, dental practices and both campaign groups. About 24 parent interviews, 10 professional interviews, 6 councillor or campaigner interviews and four focus groups separated by role. Interviews in English or with professional interpreters; vouchers for parents. Topic guide covers knowledge, actions, advice received and trust; anonymised consultation responses (COMMS-2026-08) inform but do not replace interviews.

response.designSummary: Qualitative analysis; no statistical testing. Sample size set by information power and by the quotas needed to hear each group.
response.sampleSize: Information power guides the numbers: the aim is focused, the sample is specific, established concepts (trust, legitimacy) are used and the dialogue is in-depth, so about 24 parent interviews, 10 with dental teams and school nurses and 6 with councillors or campaigners should suffice, with four focus groups to test emerging themes. At least 12 of the 24 parents come from the two most deprived quintiles, and at least 4 interviews use interpreters. Recruitment continues past these numbers only if a quota group yields no new themes in its last three interviews.
response.primaryAnalysis: Reflexive thematic analysis of transcripts, coded by two analysts for a third of transcripts and by one thereafter, with themes developed across groups and compared by deprivation and role.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Framework matrix comparing themes by participant group; the anonymised consultation responses are coded with the same framework as context.

response.risks: Low physical risk. Social risks are real: participants may fear being identified with one side in a small town, and public health staff may be seen as campaigning. Interviews are confidential, quotes are anonymised and checked for identifying details, and the team takes no role in the consultation.
response.consent: Written informed consent after information in plain language and translated where needed; separate consent for focus groups; the right to withdraw until analysis begins.
response.data: Recordings transcribed and deleted after checking; transcripts pseudonymised and stored on the university's secure server; anonymised consultation responses used under COMMS-2026-08.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: families in the most deprived neighbourhoods, those with limited English and those not registered with a dentist carry the most risk and are least heard; quotas, interpreters, vouchers and recruitment through children's centres address this.
response.effectiveness: The study shows what families understand and need; it cannot show whether cessation caused more decay.
response.efficiency: About 40 interviews within budget; focus groups test themes cheaply.
response.grants: None needed; a later evaluation of communication materials could seek regional funding.
response.partnerships: Children's centres, school nurses, local dental practices, both campaign groups and two parent advisers.
response.rebPath: Application to the regional research ethics committee submitted on 2026-09-01 (REC-2026-0412); no fieldwork before approval, which is the unknown gate that keeps the accepted decision blocked.

response.summary: Confidential interviews on a polarised topic with safeguards against identification and partisanship.

response.discussion: The discussion will relate the themes to the council's 2027 consultation and to advice from dental teams, and will re-examine the sampling rationale in light of the corrected parent survey.
response.limitations: One town; views may shift over time; one cited source was corrected after the design was accepted.
